name: Koschei's Needle
description: Needle in which the Russian fairy-tale villain Koschei the Deathless hides his soul, so that he cannot be killed while it remains intact. In Afanasyev's collected tales the needle lies inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a hare, and the hare inside a chest locked on an island oak; the hero must open each container in turn and break the needle to destroy Koschei. The motif recurs across Slavic and wider folklore, and variants replace the needle with a flower, a spider or a bird's egg. Folklorists class it among the 'external soul' tales, in which a being stores its life force outside its body for safety; the moment the chain of containers is broken, the villain collapses and dies. The needle is therefore the hinge of the whole story, and the hero's task becomes one of patience and sequence rather than of strength.
material: iron needle (in the tale, nested in egg, duck, hare, chest)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Koschei the Deathless)

name: Baba Yaga's Mortar and Pestle
description: Iron mortar and pestle ridden by Baba Yaga, the witch of Russian fairy tales, who flies over the forest in her mortar, sweeping away her trail with a broom and driving the mortar onward with the pestle. In Afanasyev's tales she is called 'Baba Yaga the Bone Leg' and travels in this way; the mortar, pestle and broom are among the most iconic props of Russian folk narrative. Folklorists note that the mortar echoes the work of grain-pounding and the boundary between the farmstead and the wild, fitting the witch who lives at the edge of the forest. She is sometimes said to fly at great speed, using the pestle as her engine and the broom to erase her traces so that pursuers cannot follow. The trio of mortar, pestle and broom has passed into art, film and illustration wherever Baba Yaga appears, and remains instantly recognisable even outside Slavic tradition.
material: iron (in the tales)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Baba Yaga tales)

name: Firebird's Feather
description: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. In Afanasyev's tale the feather, and later the bird itself, is sought as a task set by the tsar; the radiant Firebird became a favourite motif of Russian decorative art. The feather is usually the first test: the hero who takes it must then capture the living bird, often with a golden cage, and afterwards the horse with the golden mane and the fair princess Vasilisa. Because the bird is otherworldly, its feather is sometimes said to burn whatever it touches and to heal the sick if kept near. The motif later inspired Stravinsky's 1910 ballet 'The Firebird', which made the glowing feather a worldwide image of Russian fairy-tale art.
material: luminous gold feather (tale object)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('The Firebird')

name: Vasilisa's Doll
description: Small wooden doll given to Vasilisa by her dying mother in the Russian fairy tale, which eats a morsel of the girl's food and helps her perform impossible tasks so that she survives her cruel stepmother and Baba Yaga. Recorded in Afanasyev's collection as 'Vasilisa the Beautiful', the doll is the helper-object of the tale, a folk counterpart to the magical helpers of later European fairy tales. The mother's blessing is essential: the doll works only for Vasilisa, must be fed a little food, and loses its power if others discover it. When Baba Yaga sets the impossible tasks of sorting grain, cleaning the hut and weaving cloth, the doll completes them overnight, and the witch herself wonders how the girl succeeds. The doll is sometimes said to carry the soul of the dead mother watching over her daughter; folklorists read it as motherly care transformed into a protective object.
material: small wooden doll (tale object)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('Vasilisa the Beautiful')

name: Gusli (Russian Psaltery)
description: Ancient Russian plucked zither, a shallow trapezoid or helmet-shaped board with gut or metal strings, played by the epic singers who performed the byliny. The legendary Novgorod merchant Sadko of the byliny plays the gusli so well that the Sea Tsar summons him to the underwater palace; the instrument is attested in chronicles, miniatures and archaeological finds from Novgorod. Excavated Novgorod gusli date from the 11th to the 14th centuries and were carved from a single block of wood, often with a decorated sound hole. In the bylina Sadko's playing so delights the Sea Tsar that the hero is offered a bride among the sea maidens, and when the gusli breaks the music stops and the underwater court falls silent. The instrument also accompanied ritual song and dance, and it survived among folk musicians into the 19th century, when it was revived for concert and ethnographic performance.
material: wood, gut or metal strings
source: Novgorod archaeological finds; byliny of Sadko

name: Samovar (Russian Tea Urn)
description: Metal urn with a central fire-tube used to boil water for tea, a fixture of the Russian home from the early 18th century. The great workshops at Tula and in Moscow produced brass, nickel and silver samovars; around the samovar the family gathered for the evening tea, and it became a byword for hospitality in Russian daily life and literature. A charcoal fire burns in the inner tube, keeping the surrounding water at a rolling boil while the small teapot steeps on top, and the strong tea is poured from the spigot and diluted to taste in each cup. The form spread across Russia, Ukraine and the Caucasus and eastwards through Central Asia, and travellers carried samovars on long journeys. Tula became the centre of manufacture, and the city's museum of samovars preserves hundreds of examples, from the copper kettles of the 18th century to the mass-produced factory models of the 20th.
material: brass, copper, nickel or silver
source: Tula State Museum of Samovars; Russian Museum of Decorative Arts

name: Balalaika (Russian Triangular Lute)
description: Three-stringed Russian lute with a characteristic triangular body, plucked or strummed to accompany folk songs and dances. The balalaika became a symbol of Russian folk music in the 19th century, when Vasily Andreyev standardised its sizes into a whole family of instruments; it is played solo and in orchestras, and its bright, percussive tone carries well in open-air music-making. The body is usually of spruce or maple, with three strings historically of gut and now of nylon or metal, and the left hand often uses a single downward stroke that produces the crisp, rhythmic drive of dance tunes. Andreyev's balalaika orchestra, founded in 1888, gave the instrument respectability and set off a craze for balalaika ensembles across Europe. It remains the best-known Russian folk instrument abroad, appearing in concert halls, films and comedy routines alike, and its solo repertoire is still taught in Russian music schools.
material: wood, gut or nylon strings
era: attested from the 17th century; standardised late 19th century
source: Russian folk music tradition; Andreyev's balalaika orchestra (1888)

name: Kokoshnik (Russian Women's Headdress)
description: Crest-shaped ceremonial headdress of Russian women, a stiff crown of brocade, velvet or silk embroidered with pearls, gold thread and beads. Worn over the braids from the 17th century, the kokoshnik varied by region, from horned and high-crested to flat-topped forms, and marked the married woman; after Peter the Great's court reforms it survived as festive wear in the provinces. The word derives from 'kokosh', the old Russian name for a hen or cockerel, from the crest-like shape, and the headdress was worn at weddings and church festivals together with the best dress. Regional types carry distinct names, such as the one-horned kika of Tula and the morshen of the north, each built on a stiffened cardboard or birch-bark base covered in rich fabric. Museums hold examples sewn with river pearls, and the form has been revived on the stage, in film and in neo-Russian fashion, making it one of the most recognisable images of Russian national costume.
material: brocade, velvet, silk, pearls, gold thread
source: Russian Ethnographic Museum; historic Russian dress studies

name: Rushnyk (Ukrainian Ritual Cloth)
description: Embroidered ritual cloth of Ukraine woven from linen or hemp and decorated with geometric and floral embroidery at both ends. The rushnyk hangs on icons, frames doors and windows, joins the couple's hands at weddings and lines the coffin at funerals; its patterns carry protective meaning, and a woman's rushnyk collection testified to her skill. Made on the home loom and embroidered with cotton or silk thread in red, black and white, the cloths are kept for decades and passed down through families as heirlooms. The name shares its root with 'ruka', the hand, for the towel used to wipe the hands, yet the ceremonial rushnyk is never used for ordinary washing. In the wedding the bride presents rushnyky to the groom's family, and the cloth laid under the couple's feet is kept as a talisman for the marriage. Ethnographic museums treat the rushnyk as a central emblem of Ukrainian material culture.
material: linen or hemp, embroidery thread
source: Ivan Honchar Museum; Ukrainian ethnographic collections

name: Pysanka (Ukrainian Decorated Egg)
description: Ukrainian Easter egg decorated by the wax-resist method: a stylus called pysachok draws lines of hot beeswax on the shell, which is then dyed in successive colours, ending with the wax melted away to reveal the pattern. Pysanky bear solar, plant and animal motifs linked to spring rebirth, and eggs were kept in the house as protective charms. The practice is ancient, and ornamented eggs from the region date back to pre-Christian times; the egg is sometimes said to carry the hope of the resurrection and the turning of the year. Each region keeps its own colours and motifs, from the black-red-white geometry of the Kyiv area to the floral wreaths of Podillia. Making pysanky is a seasonal craft concentrated in the days before Easter, and women guard their own family patterns. Today the craft is taught in schools and workshops and has spread around the world with the Ukrainian diaspora.
material: hen's egg, beeswax, natural dyes
source: Ukrainian pysanka tradition; Lviv Ethnography Museum collections

name: Bandura (Ukrainian Zither-Lute)
description: Plucked string instrument of Ukraine combining a lute's neck with a zither-like soundboard holding up to several dozen strings, played by folk singers called bandurysts and kobzars. The kobzar tradition of singing epic dumy to the bandura is among Ukraine's most distinctive musical heritage; the instrument descends from the older kobza and spread across Ukraine from at least the 18th century. In performance the player fingers the melody on the neck while sweeping across the accompaniment strings on the soundboard, producing a resonant, harp-like texture. The blind kobzars who wandered the villages singing historical ballads were famed for long improvisations, and the term 'kobzar' became a byword for the wandering epic singer. The instrument survived the suppression of the kobzar guilds in the Soviet era and is now taught in conservatories, performed in ensembles, and honoured at festivals of Ukrainian music.
material: wood body, gut or metal strings
era: attested from at least the 18th century
source: Ukrainian bandura tradition; studies of the dumy epics

name: Slutsk Belt
description: Woven silk belt produced from the mid-18th century at the Slutsk manufactory of the Radziwiłł family in present-day Belarus, worn with the kontusz coat by Polish-Lithuanian nobility. Double-sided silk with gold and silver thread, floral and checkered borders and maker's marks woven into the ends; genuine Slutsk belts were prized across the Commonwealth and are now a national symbol of Belarus. The manufactory, founded around 1758, employed weavers from Persia and the Ottoman lands, and its belts imitated the prized sashes of the East so well that Polish nobles asked for 'Slutsk belts' in place of Persian ones. A belt was up to four metres long and folded several times around the waist, with one side in bright colours for daily wear and the other in sombre tones for mourning. Production ended in the 1840s, but the pattern entered heraldry and modern Belarusian imagery, and the belt is reproduced in museum workshops today.
material: silk, gold and silver thread
maker: Slutsk manufactory, founded by Michał Kazimierz Radziwiłł
source: National Museum of Belarus, Slutsk belt collection

name: Latvian Josta (Woven Belt)
description: Ornamental belt woven by Latvian women on a small rigid loom, patterned with geometric symbols of the sun, moon and stars and the zigzag josta motif, worn by men to hold shirt and breeches. A full-length josta measures several metres and is wound twice around the waist; its weaving is a living craft, and the Latvian National Centre for Culture keeps a register of master weavers. The belt is part of the national costume worn at song festivals, and its symbols are read as protective signs: the sun for light, the grass snake for the household, and the endless repeating band for continuity. Traditionally the josta was a woman's gift, woven for her husband or son, and a richly patterned belt showed both the weaver's skill and the family's standing. Museum examples from the 19th century show the standard red, white and green palette with the black zigzag that gives the belt its name.
material: wool or linen yarn
source: Latvian National Centre for Culture (josta pattern register)

name: Romanian Blouse (Ie)
description: Traditional Romanian blouse, the ie, a linen or cotton chemise whose sleeves and shoulders carry dense geometric embroidery; the shoulder ornament, altița, marks the wearer's region and status. Worn in village dress through the 20th century, the ie entered art and fashion through painters such as Matisse; in 2022 UNESCO inscribed 'the traditional blouse with altița' on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. The embroidery is worked in cross-stitch on the sleeves, collar and hem, with colours and motifs varying by region, and the altița, a wide band of stitching running from shoulder to sleeve, is the most valued part. Young women prepared several blouses in their trousseau, and the finest were sewn with the thinnest linen and the most intricate patterns. A 'Day of the Romanian Blouse' is celebrated every year on 24 June, and the ie has been adopted as a modern symbol of Romanian identity in fashion and design.
material: linen or cotton, cotton or silk thread
source: UNESCO ICH 'The traditional blouse with altița' (2022, Romania)

name: Cimbalom (Hungarian Hammered Dulcimer)
description: Large hammered dulcimer of Hungary, a trapezoid box with rows of metal strings struck by small wooden hammers; the concert cimbalom developed in Budapest in the 1870s. It appears in Romani music and in the works of composers such as Kodály and Bartók, while its village relatives are played across Eastern Europe; the Hungarian word cimbalom names the whole family of hammered dulcimers. The instrument has two registers of strings crossing the soundboard, a damping pedal to stop the ringing, and a boxy, resonant tone that carries clearly in a hall. Virtuoso players command a solo repertoire, and the cimbalom is also used in gypsy bands, where it once set the tempo and the harmony. Since the 19th century it has travelled to the Americas with emigrants, and it remains a fixture of Hungarian folk and folk-influenced classical music.
material: wood box, metal strings, wooden hammers
era: concert form from the 1870s; village instruments older
source: Hungarian cimbalom tradition; Kodály and Bartók repertoire

name: Polish Pisanki (Decorated Eggs)
description: Polish Easter eggs decorated by several regional techniques: batik wax-resist (pisanki), scratch-carving, and the solid raspberry-dyed eggs called byki. Patterns of rays, stars and plant sprigs vary by region, with Kraków, Łowicz and the Opoczno district known for distinct styles; eggs were exchanged at Easter as gifts and kept in the home as charms. The name comes from 'pisać', to write or paint, since the wax is drawn onto the shell with a pin dipped in a funnel of molten wax. The techniques include the kraszanki boiled in onion skins for a uniform red-brown, the skrobanki scratched through the dyed shell to reveal white, and the pisanki written with wax in several colours. In folk belief the decorated egg brought health and protection, and at Easter it was shared at the table and given to godchildren. The craft is still practised across Poland, and regions hold competitions in the days before Easter.
material: hen's egg, beeswax, dyes, scratching tools
source: National Ethnographic Museum, Warsaw; Polish ethnographic collections

name: Ciupaga (Podhale Axe-Staff)
description: Small axe with a long wooden haft carried by the highlanders (górale) of the Polish Tatra mountains as a walking staff, herding tool and dance prop. The ciupaga's haft is often carved, and highlanders strike it on the floor in the energetic zbójnicki dance; it accompanies the shepherd's life of the Podhale region and is a recognised emblem of Tatra highland culture. Its head resembles an ice-axe, with a short blade on one side and a rounded butt on the other, and it serves as a climbing stick, a lever, and a defence against wolves and bears. The wooden haft, up to a metre long, is a canvas for ornament: stars, suns and geometric bands are burned or incised into the ash or beech wood. The zbójnicki, the dance of the historic brigands who sheltered in the mountains, is performed with the ciupaga raised and struck, and the object remains a proud mark of highland identity worn on formal dress.
material: steel blade, ash or beech haft
source: Podhale highland culture studies; Tatra Museum, Zakopane

name: Dombra (Kazakh Two-String Lute)
description: Pear-shaped, long-necked two-stringed plucked lute of the Kazakh steppe, the country's signature instrument. Solo instrumental pieces (kuy) performed on dombra are central to Kazakh identity and the tradition of Dombra Kuy is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List. Legendary kuishi like Qurmangazy composed famous kuys on it, and epic singers accompanied their tales with the instrument. The two gut or nylon strings are tuned a fourth apart, and the player fingers the melody with one hand while striking both strings with the other, giving the kuy its driving rhythm and its dialogue between high and low voices. The dombra is sometimes said to have been created by Korkyt Ata, the legendary sage who, fleeing death, hung a string over the waters and let its note speak for him. Dombra-playing is taught in schools, and the instrument appears in the emblem of the National Philharmonic and in the hands of every Kazakh ensemble.
material: wood (often apricot or pine), gut/nylon strings
era: ancient; kuy tradition documented from 19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Kazakh traditional art of Dombra Kuy' (2014); Kazakh National Museum

name: Qobyz (Kazakh Horsehair Fiddle)
description: Bowed two-string fiddle of shamans and bakhsy among the Kazakhs, carved from a single piece of wood with horsehair strings and a leather-covered resonator. Legend names Korkyt Ata as its inventor; its sound was held to drive away evil spirits, sickness and death. The qobyz remains the emblematic instrument of Kazakh epic and ritual tradition. The two thick horsehair strings are bowed like a cello, the instrument held between the knees, and its deep, wavering tone was considered the very voice of the steppe. In earlier centuries it accompanied the bakhsy, the Kazakh shaman-healer, who used its sound to enter trance and to draw the spirits of the dead; the same instrument later served the singers of heroic tales. Korkyt, who is sometimes said to have strung his kobyz with his own sinews in pursuit of immortality, gives the instrument its sacred standing, and it remains a symbol of Kazakh national music.
material: single block of wood (often apricot), horsehair strings, leather soundboard
source: Korkyt legends of the Book of Dede Korkut cycle; Qazaqstan heritage portal 'Kobyz and Korkut'; ar.culture.ru collections

name: Shanyrak (Yurt Crown)
description: The crown of the Kazakh yurt: a circular wooden rim with radiating cross-beams (uyk) that supports the roof and lets smoke and daylight pass through the top opening. Beyond architecture, the shanyrak is the foremost Kazakh symbol of home, family continuity and the nation; it stands at the centre of Kazakhstan's state emblem, and custom passes the family shanyrak to the household heir. In yurt construction the shanyrak is the keystone: curved wooden ribs are lashed to its rim, felt and ropes are laid over the frame, and the whole dwelling can be dismantled and loaded on horses in under an hour. The crossing beams radiate from a central crown, and the shanyrak appears in the wedding, where newlyweds are blessed beneath it. The word itself carries the idea of the home as a circle of kin, and a Kazakh saying holds that the strength of a family is measured by the soundness of its shanyrak.
material: wood (willow, birch, poplar), felt
source: Akorda — National Emblem of Kazakhstan; ar.culture.ru 'Yurt'

name: Saukele (Kazakh Bridal Headdress)
description: Tall conical wedding headdress of Kazakh brides, covered with silver plaques, coral, beads and gemstones, with a fur-trimmed brow and long veils. The most expensive item of a bride's dowry after the yurt, the saukele symbolised the beginning of married life; it was handed down from mother to daughter and worn until the birth of the first child. The cone is built over a stiffened cloth or felt base, wrapped in velvet or brocade, and studded with silver medallions and carnelian; a fringe of coral and pearls falls over the forehead, and long beaded tassels hang past the shoulders. The weight of a richly made saukele could reach several kilograms, and a bride might wear it only for the wedding and the following days. The name is sometimes said to come from 'sau', well-being, and 'kele', crown, for the headdress that brings fortune. Museums in Kazakhstan and Siberia hold 19th-century examples, some kept as family heirlooms for generations.
material: velvet or cloth, silver plaques, coral, beads, gold thread, fur
source: Omsk Museum of History and Regional Studies; ar.culture.ru 'Saukele'

name: Kamcha (Kazakh Whip)
description: Braided leather whip of the Kazakhs, carried by horsemen and elders as a riding tool and badge of authority. In Kazakh folklore the kamcha carried protective power: the whip of a respected man was hung near a woman in childbirth, and its crack was said to drive off evil spirits. Skilled craftsmen braid the lash from several plaited leather cords. The handle is carved of wood or bone, often ornamented with silver, and the lash tapers from the handle to a thin tip that cracks sharply in the air when snapped. In the steppe the kamcha was as much a tool of the herd as of the saddle, used to guide horses and cattle at a distance, and an elder carried it as a mark of rank and command. Kazakh custom holds that the whip is never pointed at a person, and a man leaving on a journey might hang his kamcha over the threshold as protection for the house.
material: braided leather, wood or bone handle
source: e-history.kz 'The role of the horse in Kazakh culture' (2016); Kazinform feature on whip-braiding

name: Tubeteika (Tatar Skullcap)
description: Hemispherical embroidered skullcap, the traditional headwear of Tatar men. Decorated with silk or velvet embroidery in floral and geometric patterns, the tubeteika was worn at home and in public, while the taller cone-shaped kelepush was worn outdoors. Embroidered tubeteikas were part of festive dress and remain a symbol of Tatar national identity. The cap is made of velvet or thick cotton sewn in four wedge-shaped panels, joined at the crown and embroidered by hand with gold thread, silk and beads; the ornament covers the crown and often spills over the band. In Tatar custom a man removed his tubeteika only indoors and in his own home, and a cap was sewn specially for weddings and festivals. Kazan Tatar embroidery is famous for its small, dense stitches, and 19th-century examples in museum collections show the deep red, green and gold palette typical of the region. The tubeteika is still worn by Tatar men on holidays and by performers of Tatar music.
material: velvet, silk thread, cotton
source: National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan; tatarstan.ru 'Clothes and trappings'

name: Kalfak (Tatar Women's Embroidered Cap)
description: Velvet cap worn by Tatar women, richly embroidered with gold thread, pearls and gilt coins, with a long embroidered tail or tassel hanging down the back. Part of a woman's dowry, the kalfak was the most original piece of Tatar women's festive headwear and demanded great skill in gold embroidery; unlike the man's tubeteika it marked marital status and rank. The cap is sewn in a crescent or beaked shape that sits toward the back of the head, its velvet embroidered in gold thread laid in tight couched stitches, with a pendant band falling to the shoulder. In the 19th century married and unmarried women wore different forms, and the kalfak was trimmed with pearls, sequins and small gilt coins that rattled softly as the wearer moved. Embroidering a kalfak could take weeks of exacting work, and girls prepared them as gifts within the trousseau. Kazan museums display 19th-century examples, and the kalfak is now revived in festive dress and on the stage.
material: velvet, gold thread, pearls, gilt coins
source: tatarstan.ru 'Clothes and trappings'; National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan

name: Kumgan (Tatar Copper Ewer)
description: Narrow-necked copper or brass ewer with a spout and handle used by the Tatars for water and for the ritual ablution before Muslim prayer. Made by Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), the kumgan was a symbol of the Tatar home, kept with a towelled basin and used at festivals and religious observances. Kazan and the villages of Zakazanye produced the finest examples. The ewer's long spout and slender neck pour a controlled stream, and the body is often engraved with floral or geometric ornament; some examples carry a lid and a pierced foot. The kumgan is used in the washing that precedes prayer, and its shape reflects centuries of contact between Volga Tatar craftsmen and the metalwork of Central Asia and the Middle East. In the 18th and 19th centuries the coppersmiths of Kazan and its surrounding villages supplied ewers, basins and kettles far beyond the Volga, and their work was praised at the great fairs. Museum collections preserve kumgans from the 16th to the 19th century, showing the craft's long and steady development.
material: copper, brass, silver
maker: Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), Kazan and Zakazanye workshops
source: ar.culture.ru 'Kumgan' (Tatarstan museums); National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan

name: Khomus (Yakut Jew's Harp)
description: Metal Jew's harp of the Yakut (Sakha) people, an elongated iron frame with a flexible steel tongue, played by plucking the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The khomus imitates bird calls and natural sounds, accompanied songs and held shamanic associations. Yakutsk's Khomus Museum, the republic's Khomus Day and an international festival honour it as a symbol of Sakha culture. The player holds the frame against the teeth and strikes the tongue with a finger, shaping the note with the mouth and breath, so that a single harp produces a shifting range of overtones. The khomus is among the oldest of instruments, with wooden and bone examples and a metal specimen dated around the 3rd to 1st centuries BC attributed to the Xiongnu. The Yakut khomus is sometimes said to have been made first from the wood or bone of a tree struck by lightning, and later from iron, in the shape of the horseshoe that frames the tongue. Its repertoire includes pieces for healing, for the dance, and for imitating the sounds of the taiga.
material: iron or steel frame and tongue
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Khomus'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Khomus Museum, Yakutsk

name: Serge (Yakut Carved Hitching Post)
description: Carved wooden hitching post of the Yakut (Sakha) people, set up at home and at the ysyakh summer festival, often topped with carved horse-heads. The sacred Aar Baah Serge of the festival stands on the eastern side as a symbolic world-tree, a ladder linking earth to the upper world where the aiyy deities dwell; horses are tied facing east during the celebration. The post is hewn from a single larch or birch, its foot buried deep and its upper part carved into a horse's head or into stacked, cup-shaped tiers. Around a family dwelling several serges stood, each with its use: the home post for daily tethering, the wedding post for the horse of the groom, and the sacrifice post for the white stallion offered to the sky spirits. Folklorists read the serge as the axis of the homestead, an image of the world-tree connecting the three levels of the Sakha cosmos. Carving a good serge was a mark of mastery, and old posts are preserved as ancestors' property.
material: larch wood, carved
source: Gogolev et al., 'Yakut National Holiday — Ysyakh: traditions and modernity' (Berghahn Books)

name: Bychakh (Yakut Knife)
description: Traditional knife of the Yakut (Sakha) people, with an asymmetric blade bearing a fuller on one side and a convex edge on the other, a birch-burl handle and a leather sheath. Forged by Yakut blacksmiths from local iron since pre-Russian times, it is used for carving wood, dressing hides and preparing fish and meat, an everyday tool with a remarkably constant design. The blade is set into a short, rounded handle of birch burl, and the whole knife, worn at the belt in a wooden-lined leather sheath, fits the hand so well that it can be used for hours without fatigue. Yakut smithing was famed in Siberia: local marsh iron was smelted and worked into knives, and the blacksmith's trade was held in such honour that it was treated as almost sacred. The bychakh is carried by men for nearly every task of taiga and farm life, and examples found in old burials show the same form as knives made today. It is sometimes said that a good Yakut knife is judged by its balance and by the feel of the birch-burl handle.
material: locally smelted iron, birch burl handle, leather sheath
era: ancient; similar knives found in Yakut burial grounds
source: Wikipedia 'Yakutian knife'; ar.culture.ru 'Yakutian knife'; Russian Museum of Ethnography

name: Choron (Yakut Kumys Vessel)
description: Carved wooden drinking vessel of the Yakut (Sakha) people, made from a single piece of birch or spruce burl, with a conical or rounded body and short legs. The choron is the principal ritual vessel of the ysyakh summer festival, filled with kumys and offered in honour of the aiyy deities, then shared among the celebrants; its elegant form is held to resemble a bird. The body swells gently from a small mouth and stands on three or four short carved legs, and the outer surface is often engraved with bands of geometric ornament. At the festival the first choron of kumys is raised to the sky and poured to the four directions, and the celebrants then drink in turn, some vessels holding several litres. The carving follows the grain of the burl, and the best chorons are so carefully balanced that they stand firm on uneven ground. Old examples in Sakha museums show the same proportions as those made today, the form passed down unchanged for centuries.
material: birch or spruce burl, carved
source: Gogolev et al., 'Ysyakh' (Berghahn Books); ar.culture.ru 'Choron'

name: Buryat Shaman's Drum (Hese)
description: Oval single-headed frame drum of the Buryat shaman (bo), fitted with a cross-shaped handle and a rawhide head often painted with images of animals and the world tree. Struck to summon spirits and to carry the shaman between the worlds, the drum (hese) is the central instrument of Buryat ritual practice; obtaining one marked the shaman's consecration. The frame is bent from a single strip of wood, the head is stretched over it, and the inside carries an iron cross that the shaman grips with the thumb and fingers. The drum is beaten with a padded mallet, and its rhythm varies with the rite: slow strokes for the long journeys to the upper world, quick ones for warding off hostile spirits. A new drum was consecrated at the shaman's initiation, and the first sound it made was sometimes said to reveal which ancestors' spirits would assist him. Ethnographic collections hold drums painted with the sun and moon, the tree of life and the shaman's animal helpers, each image tied to the songs he sang.
material: wooden frame, rawhide head, iron handle
source: Wierucka, 'Shamanism in the Baikal Region' (2013); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat drum'

name: Buryat Shaman's Horse-Staff
description: Ritual staff of the Buryat shaman, carved from birch wood and topped with a horse's head; senior shamans who had passed the fifth consecration carried iron-tipped versions. In Buryat belief the horse-staff served as the shaman's mount to ride through the spirit world, and it remains a recognised emblem of Buryat shamanic practice alongside the drum. The staff is held upright in the ritual tent, its butt struck on the ground to punctuate the songs, and its carved horse-head top is draped with ribbons and small bells. The iron-tipped staff was a privilege of the senior shaman, and a shaman's degree was read in part from the staff he carried and the number of drums he owned. When a shaman died, his staff and drums were sometimes left in the forest at the place of his last ritual. The custom links Buryat practice to a wide Inner Asian pattern, in which the shaman rides a staff or drum as a steed into the spirit realm.
material: birch wood, iron (senior versions)
source: Czaplicka, 'Shamanism in Siberia' (1914); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat shaman's staff'

name: Igil (Tuvan Horsehead Fiddle)
description: Two-stringed bowed fiddle of the Tuvans, its hollow wooden body covered with hide and its neck crowned with a carved horse's head. The igil accompanies khoomei throat singing and Tuvan epic song, evoking the gait and voice of a steppe horse; it is prized across Central Asia and appears in the collection of the Russian Museum of Ethnography. The two strings, traditionally of horsehair, are tuned a fifth apart and played with a bow, the instrument held upright on the knee; the sound is soft and nasal, and players imitate the walk, trot and gallop of the horse with the bow. In Tuva, 2009 was declared the Year of the Igil, and the master player Bady-Dorzhu Ondar was celebrated for carrying the instrument onto the world stage. The fiddle accompanies the long epic recitals, its repeated ostinato supporting the singer's phrases, and it is sometimes said to carry the voice of the horse that bore the hero. Today the igil is taught in Tuvan music schools and performed in ensembles around the world.
material: wooden body, hide soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Alash Ensemble; ar.culture.ru 'Igil'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Doshpuluur (Tuvan Three-String Lute)
description: Long-necked, three-stringed plucked lute of the Tuvans, with a small wooden body often carved in a canoe shape and gut or nylon strings. The doshpuluur forms a key part of Tuvan music, accompanying songs and dance and often played in duet with the igil; it is a close relative of the Altai topshur and the Mongolian tovshuur. The player plucks the strings with one hand while fretting the melody with the other, and its dry, percussive sound supports the rhythmic side of Tuvan song. It is used in folk ensembles and by throat-singers to keep the beat, and in the kargyraa style its notes double the low drone. The instrument's simple construction, from a single carved body and a hide or wooden soundboard, keeps it light enough to travel with the herder's household. In modern Tuva it is played in conservatories and by groups such as the Alash ensemble, which carry the doshpuluur's sound to concert halls abroad.
material: wood body, gut/nylon strings
source: Wikipedia 'Doshpuluur'; ar.culture.ru collections

name: Topshur (Altai Two-String Lute)
description: Two-stringed plucked lute of the Altai people, carved with a shallow bowl body, hide soundboard and gut or horsehair strings. The topshur accompanies the kaychi storytellers, who perform the great Altai heroic epics such as the Tale of Maadai-Kara; its music is bound to Altai oral tradition and is often played before the fire and during ritual. The player holds the instrument against the body and plucks with a bare hand, and the music is thought to summon the presence of the epic's heroes as the singer speaks their deeds. The two strings are sometimes tuned a fourth apart, and the tone is soft and earthy, suited to the low, long-narrative voice of the kaychi. Because the epic is sacred, the topshur is treated with care, and a player is sometimes said to warm the hide soundboard by the fire before beginning, so that the instrument will sing. Kaychi performance of Maadai-Kara can last a whole night, the topshur's ostinato carrying the story through the darkness.
material: wood body, hide soundboard, gut/horsehair strings
source: ar.culture.ru 'Topshur'; Altai kaychi tradition

name: Altai Komus (Jew's Harp)
description: Jew's harp of the Altai people, usually of metal or wood with a flexible tongue, played by strumming the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The komus is widely used for personal music and to accompany songs; its voice imitates natural sounds. It belongs to the same family of Siberian mouth harps as the Yakut khomus and the Buryat khuur. The player shapes the note with the mouth and breath, producing a low drone with ringing overtones that can mimic the wind, a running stream, or the calls of birds. In Altai tradition the komus was played by young men courting, by shepherds in the mountain pastures, and by singers practising the khoomei throat styles, and it is sometimes said that the sound of the komus carries the voice of the taiga itself. The instrument is small enough to be carried in the pocket, and its repertoire is largely improvised. Today the komus is performed at festivals, taught in music schools, and prized in the pan-Siberian revival of the mouth harp.
material: iron, brass or wood; steel tongue
source: ar.culture.ru 'Komus (Altai)'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Malitsa (Nenets Reindeer-Fur Coat)
description: Men's winter coat of the Nenets reindeer herders, sewn from reindeer skins with the fur turned inward, a hood attached inside, and worn with a belt (sok) and fur mittens. Decorated with white or red fur tufting and fur mosaic, the malitsa is made from autumn- and winter-killed reindeer and is the herders' everyday Arctic dress. Because the fur faces inward, the garment traps warm air against the body while the smooth outer hide sheds wind and snow, and the sewn-in hood protects the head without an added collar. The malitsa reaches to the knees, its hem edged with the dark leg fur of the reindeer, and the belt holds the coat closed at the waist and carries the hunter's knife and pouch. Nenets women sew the coats with sinew thread, using the tough winter hide for the body and the soft fur of young deer for trimming. In the polar cold the malitsa is sometimes said to be warm enough to sleep in, and herders keep it on even indoors.
material: reindeer hide, fur, sinew thread
source: NAO24 official Nenets Autonomous Okrug portal; ar.culture.ru Arctic collections

name: Yaranga (Chukchi Portable Dwelling)
description: Large hemispherical tent dwelling of the coastal Chukchi, built on a wooden frame of poles and whale ribs and covered with walrus skins, with reindeer hides laid inside against the cold. A family camp could stretch up to twenty metres; inside, fur-lined sleeping chambers formed separate rooms. The yaranga was central to Chukchi coastal life. Its frame is assembled from long poles set in a circle and tied at the top, with heavy walrus hides laid over the sides and secured against the wind with stones and lines; the interior is divided into a cold outer ring and a warm inner chamber, the polog, a tent of reindeer hides where the family sleeps. Reindeer-herding Chukchi carried lighter versions that could be packed on sleds and pitched in an hour, while the coastal people built the heavier skin yarangas of the sea-hunters. The yaranga is sometimes said to turn its entrance away from the wind, and travellers could enter it even without invitation. Skins and poles are still used in Chukotka today.
material: wooden poles, whale ribs, walrus skins, reindeer hides
source: ar.culture.ru 'Chukchi' (Russian Museum of Ethnography collections)

name: Chukchi Walrus-Ivory Carving
description: Carved objects of the Chukchi and Siberian Yupik of the Chukotka coast, worked from walrus tusks into harpoon heads, amulets, figurines and engraved scenes of sea-hunting and animal life. Walrus ivory carving is a hallmark of Chukchi art, celebrated by the Uelen bone-carving workshop and collected by the Russian Museum of Ethnography. The tusk is cut and sawn, then shaped with knives and polished with the hide of the walrus itself, and engravers trace outlines of hunters, walruses, whales and spirits in fine, firm lines. In the past ivory was also the material of daily life: harpoon points, toggles and needle cases were carved for use at sea, and small figurines were carried as charms. The workshop at Uelen, founded in the 1930s on the Bering coast, gathered carvers of the Chukchi and Yupik villages and gave the craft a lasting home. Ivory is sometimes said to hold the luck of the hunt, and a well-carved tusk remains a family treasure on the Chukotka coast.
material: walrus ivory (tusk)
maker: Chukchi and Siberian Yupik carvers, including the Uelen workshop
source: Wikipedia 'Walrus ivory carving'; ar.culture.ru Chukotka collections

name: Evenki Shaman's Costume
description: Ceremonial cloak of the Evenki shaman, sewn from reindeer hide and hung with iron pendants shaped as birds, fish, deer, snakes and human figures that represent the shaman's spirit-helpers, with a fringed apron and iron rattles. The costume is preserved in the collections of the Russian Museum of Ethnography and Siberian regional museums. Each pendant is forged to correspond to a spirit that the shaman called upon, and their number and variety grew with the shaman's rank and experience. The cloak is worn over the ordinary clothes with an apron and a headdress, and the iron objects ring together in motion, so that the shaman's very movements sound the spirits' presence. A new costume was made at consecration, sometimes according to the vision of an ancestor shaman, and it was kept apart from daily garments and handed down or destroyed at the shaman's death. The costume is the physical map of the Evenki spirit world, and ethnographers have used its pendants to reconstruct the lists of helpers in Evenki belief.
material: reindeer hide (rovduga), iron pendants, leather fringe
source: ar.culture.ru 'Evenk shaman costume'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Nivkh Shaman's Drum
description: Oval frame drum of the Nivkh people of Sakhalin and the Amur region, with a wooden handle, used by the shaman to accompany spirit journeys and healing rituals. Its sound marks the shaman's passage between the worlds, as recorded by ethnographers including Emiko Ohnuki-Tierney in her study of Nivkh shamanism. The drum is made with a bent wooden rim and a hide head, tightened while wet and dried over the frame, with a carved handle or cross-bar on the underside. It is beaten with a soft mallet, and the shaman uses both the strokes and the pauses to summon and question the spirits. In the bear festival, the greatest Nivkh ceremony, the drum accompanied the songs honouring the bear and the masters of the forest and sea. The Nivkh shaman served the community as healer and guide, and his drum, like his helpers, was passed on within the family line. Museum examples come mainly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the Amur peoples were collected most intensively.
material: wooden frame, hide head, wooden handle
source: Ohnuki-Tierney, 'Nivkh Shamanism' (1981); ar.culture.ru 'Nivkh drum'
